title: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
description: Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that le
body: Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday. "We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.   The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals. He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network". Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said."Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently"."It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said. Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications. Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

schema.headline: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide

title: Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment
description: Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer. The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently
body: Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer. The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently took part in the second season of the Celebrity Traitors, said cancerous cells were discovered after she attended a cervical screening in 2020.She underwent a hysterectomy, describing the experience to BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs as "horrific". "As awful as that was, it had a full stop at the end of the sentence," the 42-year-old added. "I had my five-year clear the other day. I feel so unbelievably lucky."In Sunday's episode, Fry told show host Lauren Laverne that she had delayed a cervical screening examination for months in 2020. After she attended one, the results "didn't come back for a few weeks," she said. "Then I got a call from my GP telling me they needed me to come back and do another test, and they did a biopsy."I was trying hard not to panic but when they found it was in the lymphatic system… that was when it really started to come down."The broadcaster said she was told that her chances of survival depended on the cancerous cells not having spread to her lymph nodes, although it was not clear "how bad it was at that point"."It's all about, basically, how far into your lymphatic system has it got. If it had not got into any lymph nodes, then the odds were in my favour and I had a really good chance of survival," she said.Fry explained that this meant "if it was in one it would drop to a 60% chance of survival and two – the odds would go against me and it would be a 40% chance".While in isolation in hospital following her hysterectomy, Fry said a surgeon told her that four of her lymph nodes had appeared enlarged.She added: "I was in this hospital bed on my own and no-one could come and visit me for over a week, with nothing but the sheer terrifying drop of the end of my existence in front of me – it was horrific."Fry described not being able to "think back to happy things that... have already happened because it is sad", while also not being able to "look forward to things you are hopeful about because it doesn't feel like it is there".She also said she asked her then husband to set up FaceTime in the corner of a room so she could watch their two young daughters play while she was in hospital."I didn't want them to see me, it was too much," she said.But she added: "Going through something like that I don't think I would swap it. "I think it was honestly such a gift to have that experience when you're 36 and then come out the other side of it."The presenter grew up in a working-class family and studied mathematics at University College London.She later completed a PhD in fluid dynamics, and last year became Cambridge University's first professor of the public understanding of mathematics.Fry has fronted BBC science series including The Future with Hannah Fry and The Secret Genius of Modern Life.She was banished in the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors after being exposed as a traitor.

schema.headline: Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment

title: Two die in Leeds car crash after police pursuit
description: Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds.West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, whe
body: Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds.West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, when a blue BMW 123D failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road and then crashed into a white Volkswagen Scirocco.The driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man, died at the scene. His passenger, a woman, 23, died later in hospital. Both were from York.The occupants of the BMW, a 39-year-old man from Harrogate, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.The 39-year-old is also being held on suspicion of driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis, the force confirmed.The teenagers in the BMW were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening.A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said a referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which confirmed it had started an investigation.

schema.headline: Two die in Leeds car crash after police pursuit

title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
description: Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones i
body: Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there"."Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine."It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk."On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram."Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented."Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

schema.headline: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'

title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
description: A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tool
body: A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance."I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday."I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly."It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

schema.headline: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating

title: DP World Tour Championship: Rory McIlroy claims Race To Dubai as Tyrell Hatton wins tournament
description: DP World Tour Championship final leaderboard-15 Hatton (Eng); -10 McIlroy (NI); -8 Chacarra (Spa), Lindell (Fin); -7 Olesen (Den), Reitan (Nor), Lapor
body: DP World Tour Championship final leaderboard-15 Hatton (Eng); -10 McIlroy (NI); -8 Chacarra (Spa), Lindell (Fin); -7 Olesen (Den), Reitan (Nor), Laporta (Ita), Lindberg (Swe), Perez (Fra)Selected others: -4 Wallace (Eng); -3 Rahm (Spa), Schaper (SA); Level Fleetwwod (Eng), Reed (US), Fox (NZ); +1 Rai (Eng)Full leaderboardRory McIlroy wiped away tears as he dedicated his eighth Race to Dubai victory to his ill father, Gerry.Moments after matching Colin Montgomerie's record of season-long European tour titles on Sunday, the Northern Irishman was asked about the health of his father.An emotional McIlroy revealed Gerry has been in hospital for two months after "a huge operation" - a double lung transplant - at the end of September."He's recovering well, thankfully," McIlroy told the DP World Tour."But before I left to come here to the Middle East, I went up to Cleveland to see him. He said to me: 'Go win The Race to Dubai'."This one's for him."It came after a thrilling climax at the traditional season-ending DP World Tour Championship with Tyrrell Hatton securing a commanding victory, while McIlroy pipped Spaniard Eugenio Chacarra to the overall crown.Hatton's closing six-under-par 66 helped him romp to a five-shot victory on 15 under par but most eyes were on the thrilling battle that went down to the final hole. It is the fifth successive year that McIlroy has won the award and it has drawn him level with Montgomerie, the Scot who set a mark 21 years ago that few thought would ever be matched."Yeah, double digits," smiled McIlroy when asked what would be his final target of Race to Dubai victories."I'd love to surpass Monty next year and we'll go from there."McIlroy's confidence in going along with a target shouted out by the fans surrounding the 18th green at the Earth Course in Dubai on Sunday was refreshing to hear.But he appears to be playing and talking with a little more freedom in recent years - the sort of freedom that comes as a result of finally completing the career Grand Slam and winning successive Masters titles - and leads to declarations of winning 10, or more."Winning eight Order of Merits (Race to Dubai titles) was never in my list of goals growing up," said McIlroy, who closed with a bogey-free 67 to finish on 10 under and must surely now be considered Europe's greatest golfer."I remember Monty being a stalwart of the European tour and playing with him at the London Club in 2008, so to pull up alongside him and win eight of these means the world to me."After Jon Rahm's victory in Abu Dhabi last week, fellow former LIV Golf member Hatton showed his class with a five-shot success at the Earth Course at Jumeirah Golf Estates.Hatton showed his combustible side earlier in the week but, despite later admitting to being "weirdly nervous" he appeared serene on Sunday.In the final group and knowing he couldn't win the overall Race to Dubai title, he was detached enough to block out the scramble as he strolled to his ninth DP World Tour victory - even asking an on-course reporter who was going to win as he walked from the 17th green to 18th tee.It was that head-to-head battle between Chacarra and McIlroy that dominated the tournament, a battle that, after a long hard season, came right down to the wire.Both players knew victory would win them the title. There were permutations galore for finishing second, third, or below that.Chacarra and McIlroy went toe-to-toe in and the overall lead in the rankings chopped and changed down an absorbing back nine as neither man backed down.At one juncture just one-tenth of a point separated the pair.But a late surge from Northern Ireland's McIlroy allowed him to finish runner-up behind England's Hatton in the tournament and collect enough points to edge out the gutsy Spaniard.Chacarra, who earned around $15-20m during three years as a LIV player, is in just his second season on the DP World Tour. He is the only three-time winner of this year's campaign and was desperate to add his name to compatriots Rahm and Seve Ballesteros as the third Spanish order of merit winner.After four early birdies he looked in fine shape. The pressure began to tell as he posted three bogeys in four holes around the turn. But he responded brilliantly with two more birdies to push McIlroy all the way.Chacarra, the 26-year-old world number 39, finished in a tie for third to end up second in the overall standings and earn a PGA Tour card for next season.As tough as it was this year for McIlroy to win, mainly due to playing on the PGA Tour for the first half of the season, 2027 will be even harder because there will be some big names flooding in after the collapse of LIV Golf.Rahm and Hatton are just two high-profile LIV players who are suspended from the PGA Tour for a year following their involvement with the breakaway tour. They will both have a full season on the European circuit that will give them a big advantage over McIlroy.Along with many other big names such as Sergio Garcia, Joaquin Niemann and Tom McKibbin, there's even the possibility of Bryson DeChambeau, the biggest LIV name of all, applying to join the DP World Tour for next season.The American is eligible thanks to his 2024 US Open triumph, at McIlroy's painful expense, and had to apply by the end of the Sunday of the DP World Tour Championship.After this latest addition to McIlroy's glowing CV it's hard to make a case against him being Europe's greatest ever golfer – and as he continues to find new targets to stay motivated one of them is very much to unequivocally nail down that title.Motivation was a problem in the immediate aftermath of finally ending his long wait to win the Masters in 2025 as he became just the sixth man to win the career Grand Slam.But a year later he had re-found it as he became just the fourth back-to-back Green Jacket winner with his brilliant defence at Augusta National back in April.That put him on six major titles, level with England's Sir Nick Faldo and just one behind the great Harry Vardon, whose name adorns the trophy McIlroy has just hoisted for the eighth time.Still only 37, McIlroy still has plenty of time to overhaul Montgomerie and hold the outright record for the most European number one titles – despite playing on two tours throughout the majority of his career.Targets have changed – McIlroy is not chasing the world number one spot or winning any old trophy. He's voiced his desire to focus on majors, play more in Europe and around the globe and keep stacking up these order of merit titles.An Olympic title is perhaps the only honour missing from his trophy cabinet, and he will have the chance to change that in 2028 on a familiar Riviera Country Club Course, which is a regular stop-off on the PGA Tour and where he finished second a this year's Genesis Invitational.He will be attempting to become the first man to win three Masters in a row next April, before the US Open at Pebble Beach and Open Championship at St Andrews offer great chances at venues McIlroy knows he can thrive on.McIlroy has won six Ryder Cups as a stalwart for Europe and is just seven points behind all-time leader Sergio Garcia.But even if the Northern Irishman quit the game right now he's already built a more than compelling argument that he's the greatest player the continent has ever seen.Watch highlights of Sunday's final round on BBC 2 and BBC iPlayer from 16:15 GMT (UK only)

schema.headline: DP World Tour Championship: Rory McIlroy claims Race To Dubai as Tyrell Hatton wins tournament

title: Scotland 15-12 Australia - report
description: Nations Championship Scotland (12) 15Tries: M Fagerson, Dempsey Con: Russell Pens: Russell Australia (5) 12Tries: Potter, Jorgensen Con: DonaldsonScot
body: Nations Championship Scotland (12) 15Tries: M Fagerson, Dempsey Con: Russell Pens: Russell Australia (5) 12Tries: Potter, Jorgensen Con: DonaldsonScotland edged a dull Nations Championship encounter against Australia at Murrayfield, a game that brought rugby fans crashing back down to earth after the brilliance of France's win against South Africa on Friday and the jaw-dropping wonder of Wales beating the All Blacks on Saturday.Matt Fagerson, an impressive juggernaut, and Jack Dempsey scored for Scotland, Harry Potter got one for Australia, all in the first half hour. We waited another 47 minutes before Finn Russell banged over a penalty to make it 15-5. Max Jorgensen's converted try with seconds remaining narrowed the gap. A little flurry at the end of a hugely disappointing, attritional Test.Apart from isolated moments, it was a game of turnovers, missed opportunities and a terrible absence of anything resembling class. Compliment the grunt, but…It was chaos. Every breakdown was a lottery, an ugly dogfight. The longer it went on, the more Australia became serial offenders. That game-clinching penalty from Russell was on the back of multiple Wallaby breakdown offences.There were some seriously creative and pacy players out there but we hardly saw them. Precious little fast ball, precious little buzz from two teams who are well capable of excitement. Neither attack sparked never mind fired. The final whistle came as something of a blessing.Scotland suffered a blow even before the first whistle when captain Sione Tuipulotu was ruled out with a knee injury. Tom Jordan replaced him in the midfield and Rory Darge took over the leadership role. Both are stand-up operators, but any Scotland team without Tuipulotu is a weaker outfit.Huge question marks hung over the pair before the start - Scotland having been blown away by the All Blacks last weekend as the Wallabies went down in flames at Twickenham. Depending on how it went - Scotland were warm favourites - this was going to be some sort of redemption for one and all sorts of retribution for the other. All of that was in the balance right until the end.Scotland now move above Wales into fourth in the northern hemisphere table, but their lack of a bonus point on Sunday could cost them. They'll take the win, though.In the scrappiest encounter, the home side drew first blood. They owned the ball in the early moments, wasted one opportunity to score off a lineout maul, but then struck at the second time of asking.Finn Russell started it all with a lovely grubber that had Carter Gordon in trouble. It eventually led to a scrum and men over for Scotland. An isolated Fagerson on the right touchline had been calling for it for what must have felt like an age to him. When it did come, he had the easiest job of sliding over.Russell missed the conversion, but he missed something - or somebody - else just after and it proved costly. One of the many things holding Scotland back is how easy they are to score against - and here was another case for the prosecution.Rob Valetini and Gordon helped put the Wallabies on the front foot but, when they swept to the left touchline, the whole thing might have come to a halt had Russell made his tackle on Potter. He didn't - and the wing ran on to finish with class.Scotland thought they'd scored just after but the ball was deemed out of play - a marginal call - when Kyle Steyn mid-air volleyed to Graham, who touched down. Another injury befell the Scots midway through the opening half when Scott Cummings was replaced by Max Williamson. The Scots scored their second try soon after. Too much power in the phases and Dempsey drove over against the nation he once represented.Russell made it 12-5 and it stayed that way despite Billy Pollard being driven over from a lineout maul. The Wallabies were done for obstruction.The pre-match billing talked about a thrilling try-fest but it was low-key and error-strewn. You expected Scotland to bring their usual ambition but, if anything, they were conservative. The Wallabies tried to play more rugby, but their game was riddled with mistakes, too. It was chaos out there for large parts of it. Bodies everywhere. A million big hits. Just an awful absence of quality.Paris on Friday, this was not. Cardiff on Sunday, it was not either.Pollard got binned for going high on Blair Kinghorn early in the new half but Scotland could do nothing in those precious 10 minutes. They butchered a big opportunity from a close-range lineout - losing their own throw - then won it back and got turned over at the breakdown.Scotland played much of the second half in Aussie territory but only had those three Russell points to show for it. Just as well.Australia scored in the last seconds when Jorgensen ran in after a beautiful offload from Jeremy Williams. Ben Donaldson put over the conversion to make it 15-12. Too little, too late for the visitors. Just. Scotland survived. After two days of Nations Championship rugby that will live long in the memory, this one will have faded in the time it took fans to reach the car park.

title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
description: Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.The country's Isl
body: Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September. The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage. Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

schema.headline: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack

title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
description: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year,
body: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the  company says.Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

schema.headline: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says

title: The lessons in handshaking and eye contact preparing pupils for the world of work
description: Schools and colleges across England are legally required to have a careers programme, including expanded opportunities for work experience, and to use
body: Schools and colleges across England are legally required to have a careers programme, including expanded opportunities for work experience, and to use the updated Gatsby Benchmarks, external to structure their careers education.The Gatsby Foundation's Beth Jones, who developed the guidance, says the more careers education benchmarks a school achieves, the less likely it is their students will leave as Neet."Careers guidance cannot solve every barrier young people face, but it is an important part of helping them navigate their futures successfully," she says. There is no doubt that improving careers education and giving pupils more vocational options is part of the plan for schools, but it is not the whole picture for solving the Neet crisis. As Milburn himself pointed out in his interim report, external earlier this year, from the moment a child arrives at school at age four, the system can predict "who is most likely to fail".A child starting school without basic "school-ready" skills like potty training at ages four or five is nearly three times as likely to be Neet by the time they reach 16 or 17 years old.Pupils with special educational needs, from poorer backgrounds, or those with mental health issues are also more likely to be Neet. The problem might not be identifying the pupils that need help, but finding the funding to help them. The Institute for Fiscal Studies warned that a "one-size-fits-all approach" to the Neet crisis was "unlikely to work, given the very different circumstances of young people who are Neet".It says a "key question for the government will be how much they are willing to invest in the short run in the hope of a pay-off in future years".

schema.headline: The lessons in handshaking and eye contact preparing pupils for the world of work

title: Women's Super League: London City's 'bravery' paying off in top three pursuit
description: A sold-out away end helped fill out the 32,000-strong crowd at the Emirates on Sunday as many hoped for an end-to-end encounter.They were not disappoi
body: A sold-out away end helped fill out the 32,000-strong crowd at the Emirates on Sunday as many hoped for an end-to-end encounter.They were not disappointed as fearless London City showed bravery against an Arsenal side who played with a spark following their 1-1 draw with Barcelona.The visitors were helped out by Arsenal's wastefulness - the Gunners had 17 shots and only converted one - but London City caused plenty of problems of their own.Maestre said after their defeat by Manchester City that their opponents showed more experience and know-how but against Arsenal, his side matured.They were under pressure early on and fell a goal down thanks to Frida Maanum's opener but it took just 98 seconds for Izzy Goodwin to equalise for London City.That killed Arsenal's momentum and when the pressure increased again from the hosts in the second half, goalkeeper and player of the match Mary Earps stepped up to make crucial saves."The performance was there. We had the chances to score and get a better result but Arsenal had chances too. The game was very open," said Maestre. "The way we faced and challenged every circumstance in the game shows we are here, and able to play with that mentality in these big games."We came here to take risks. Our energy was good. We were brave and weren't scared about the context or the opponent. "We tried to play as if we were at home. I always want to feel that my teams are brave and go for the win."That bravery showed as Alexia Putellas came close twice with long-range efforts, Goodwin could have been onside when she was played in behind later on.London City hit the crossbar through substitute Delphine Cascarino and had 14 shots compared to Arsenal's 17, including four inside the box.Arsenal are still yet to win at home this season in the WSL but this was still an impressive showing from London City, who came to the Emirates to play.But while they were willing to take risks, they were smarter than they were against Manchester City, choosing when to press aggressively and when to hold off."We tried to match the pace of the ball and not expose ourselves as much to the players that Arsenal have," added Maestre. "We were trying to mix the moments we were more clinical in our press. We made some adjustments at half-time and were much better at recognising those."London City are backed by US billionaire Michele Kang and that has made a big difference in the transfer market.They recruited superstars Alexia Putellas, Mary Earps, Mapi Leon and Kadidiatou Diani in the summer.Such is their depth that high-flying Spaniard Lucia Corrales, the dangerous Cascarino and England international Freya Godfrey came off the bench. Those individual talents have made a difference and on Sunday it was goalkeeper Earps who took the plaudits, claiming the player of the match award.She made crucial saves late on as Arsenal pushed ferociously for a winner, tipping Maanum's effort onto the crossbar and blocking her shot from close range.Earps had to bide her time for the number one shirt after making the switch from Paris St-Germain this summer but has started the past three WSL games."Mary is a very strong character and is much more than the things we see in terms of the performance," said Maestre. "She has experience, and energy that you can bring to every part in the process and not just the things we see in the matches. "I think the energy that she brings to the position is massive and has a massive impact. I'm very pleased with her."Watching on in the stands was England boss Sarina Wiegman who will have been pleased with the display from goalscorer Goodwin.The 23-year-old got the better of England captain Leah Williamson when she fooled her with quick feet and fired the ball into the back of the net, making it 1-1.She is proof that competition for places in the London City starting XI is pushing players on and that their depth is improving each week."I think Izzy is becoming a more mature player. She has the inner competition and the signings sometimes push you to bring 100% every time," added Maestre. "She is committed to keep pushing and, with the performances she is having, why not [earn an England call-up]?"Izzy is moving forward in the ways she can take advantage and that commitment is the way she is reaching those performances. I'm very proud of her."

schema.headline: Women's Super League: London City's 'bravery' paying off in top three pursuit

title: Trident submarine returns home after record-breaking undersea patrol
description: Image caption, Crew members stood atop HMS Vengeance as it travelled up Gare Loch BySteven Godden and Calum WatsonBBC ScotlandA Royal Navy submarine c
body: Image caption, Crew members stood atop HMS Vengeance as it travelled up Gare Loch BySteven Godden and Calum WatsonBBC ScotlandA Royal Navy submarine carrying Trident nuclear missiles has returned to its Scottish base after a record-breaking 217 days spent submerged on patrol. The 140-strong crew of HMS Vengeance have spent the tour in almost total isolation beneath the surface after setting out from Faslane, near Helensburgh, Argyll and Bute, on 12 April.Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome them home after the longest deployment at sea for a British vessel.The typical patrol length for the UK's Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines has more than doubled in recent years, with six-month durations now routine due to a shortage of seaworthy vessels.Crew members could be seen standing on HMS Vengeance as it travelled up Gare Loch earlier, accompanied by some smaller Naval support vessels and tug boats.The vessel was encrusted in marine growth and some of its sound-absorbing tiles were missing.HMS Vengeance was expected back at Faslane last weekend, but that was reported to have been delayed, external when the submarine replacing it on patrol had to return to base to fix a technical fault. The head of the navy, First Sea Lord Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, praised the dedication of  submariners in keeping Nato safe at a conference last week in Oslo, but said the UK must do better at maintaining the fleet.Streeting said it "doesn't sit lightly" with him that crews were being asked to serve longer than intended.He said: "It makes me feel even more indebted to the crew for the service they've given to the country, for the commitment they show, the dedication, the professionalism, the expertise."I think the whole country can be extraordinarily proud of our submariners and of our nuclear deterrent."Since 1969 the UK has always had at least one ballistic missile-armed submarine patrolling at sea in order to provide a "nuclear deterrent". The logic is that if Britain was under nuclear attack, it could launch a retaliatory strike on the aggressor, a concept known as mutually-assured destruction. The four 492ft (150m) long Vanguard-class submarines can carry up to 16 Trident missiles, each capable of delivering multiple warheads which are several times more powerful than the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima in 1945. Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome the crew homeIn order to avoid detection the submarines remain submerged and in radio silence throughout the patrol because a transmission could give away their position.But they can ascend to shallower depths and receive encoded messages via a floating wire antenna or communications buoy. Crews have little contact with the loved ones apart from the "Familygram" - a 120-word message that arrives weekly, and they are not permitted to reply. Messages are vetted and bad news from home can be withheld if it might jeopardise the operational effectiveness of a crew member.Depending on the sea state they may be able to listen to radio bulletins. Most of the crew work in shifts of six hours on, six hours off and sleep in narrow bunks, sometimes nine to a cabin.Submariners returning from long patrols are said to find the outside world smells strange or even overwhelming because they have become so used to filtered air. Their distance perception could also be affected by living in such a confined space for so long and they are advised not to drive for a few days while they adjust. Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, HMS Vanguard, seen here at Faslane, is thought to have set the previous Navy record for the longest patrol when it returned in April after 205 days at seaThe Vanguard-class boats were commissioned in the 1990s with an expected service life of 25 years but are now expected to serve for up to 40 years before the first Dreadnought-class submarines start replacing them in the early 2030s. Streeting said that program was "on track" and that it was important to get those vessels out "as soon as possible".Patrols used to typically last three months but in recent years this has stretched to six or more because at least one of the boats has been out of action for refit or repairs. A major overhaul of HMS Vanguard at Devonport Dockyard in Plymouth dragged on for seven years before it returned to service in 2022. HMS Victorious is currently in dry dock undergoing a £560m "deep maintenance" that began in 2023, leaving only Vengeance, Vigilant and Vanguard operational.The previous record for a Royal Navy continuous undersea patrol is reported to have been set by Vanguard in April when it returned to Faslane after 205 days away. The patrol lengths of Russian or Chinese submarines are not known, but most navies are believed to send their vessels out for far shorter durations.

schema.headline: Trident submarine returns home after record-breaking undersea patrol

title: Pat McFadden backs legal right to job support for young people
description: The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.Pat McFadden
body: The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed.But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers. It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans.Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade.However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year.Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness. How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted.Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service.Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this."He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to."He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today".Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added.Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending.But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs".She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing.Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said:a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for governmentGPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to workministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage.From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently.It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year.

schema.headline: Pat McFadden backs legal right to job support for young people

title: Holly Humberstone on her identity crisis - and struggle being compared to other pop stars
description: Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'Image source, Silken WeinbergImage caption, Holly Humberstone says she was h
body: Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'Image source, Silken WeinbergImage caption, Holly Humberstone says she was having an identity crisis on a weekly basisByMusic correspondentYou might know her as a pop star, endorsed by everyone from Taylor Swift to Sam Fender, but Holly Humberstone has a secret double life. In her spare time, the singer-songwriter is literally a cat burglar."We've stolen one of our neighbours' cats by accident," she laughs, in a Zoom call from her fixer-upper in New Cross, south-east London. "He's a tiny little black cat who's come into our garden and simply chosen us."Under the slightest scrutiny, however, her story crumbles like a biscuit in a hot cup of tea."OK, we've been coercing him into the house with treats," she admits. "He's just so cute."But we're not trying to keep him. We literally push him out every night."Humberstone's excuse for this feline felony is that, last year, her parents sold her childhood home in Lincolnshire, external and moved to Wales  – taking her pets with them.One, a cat called Tsuki, had even been immortalised in the song Lucy as a confidante who listens to her problems but "never judges"."Oh, she knows some secrets!" laughs the singer. "I'm so glad she can't talk.""We actually tried to bring her to London with us, but she's a countryside cat and she hated it so much. We had to send her to Wales where she can be free and frolic."Her parents' relocation was disruptive for the human Humberstones, too. Their house, a "freezing cold, falling down" property 20 minutes outside of Grantham, played a huge part in the singer's success.Her early EPs were all written there, inspiring the "wonky sonics" of her indie-leaning pop sound. The 2021 single Haunted House is even dedicated to the "friendly" spirits who inhabited the property."It's a place I always felt I could go back to, to remind myself of who I am," she says. Instead, she spent 2025 "packing up 23 years of stuff my family and I had accumulated", from her old ballet shoes and poetry books to forgotten bits of jewellery.Image source, Holly HumberstoneImage caption, The singer shared photos of her old bedroom, and the artefacts she'd rediscovered, while clearing out her parents' "haunted house" in Grantham (pictured, left).The process was unsettling. Already grappling with the idea of leaving childhood behind, Humberstone found herself literally throwing away her past."I felt uprooted. I was having some sort of identity crisis almost weekly," she says.So she did what she's always done, and poured those feelings into her second album, Cruel World, which entered the UK charts at number four earlier this year."Writing these songs felt like building myself a little shield and a kind of safety bubble," she says. "There's an escapist, fantasy element to so much of the album."Maybe that's true, but Humberstone has always had the ability to locate a song's emotional core, and the lyrics on Cruel World don't disappoint."To lose somebody is to know you're only human, honey," she sings on To Love Somebody, external, soothing her elder sister as she endures an agonising break-up.Undeterred by that heartbreak, she throws herself headfirst into a new affair on Die Happy, external, declaring: "Hit the gas, I want it fast, want it reckless."But the most revealing song is the closing track, Beauty Pageant, external.Fragile and raw, it's the sound of Humberstone in her dressing room, addressing the woman in the mirror who'd "die for the applause" but who struggles with the impossible beauty standards imposed on female artists.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Humberstone's biggest songs include Falling Asleep At The Wheel, The Walls Are Way Too Thin, Die Happy and Scarlett"That's a song that I wasn't really setting out to write," she confesses."Writing about other people often feels easier than turning the magnifying glass on yourself."The lyrics, she says, draw on a "very specific" mindset she acquired at her all-girls school in Grantham."It was drilled into me: You're all in competition. You're only rewarded if you're the best. And if you're not, you're worthless."The experience "really warped the way I view other girls", she says.Musical success made it worse. After winning the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, Humberstone found herself competing with megastars, even though her music leaned towards the alternative side of pop."I'm a very small fish and I recognise that, but suddenly I was in meetings being compared to all these people on my label's roster, who are on a completely different scale," she says."It's something I really, really struggled with in the early days and it's something I've really had to unlearn."Nowadays, Humberstone has stopped benchmarking herself against her peers, recognising that the need for validation never fades."I don't think that there's a point I could get to, or an award that I could win, where these feelings would disappear," she says."Everybody feels like they've still got something to prove, so I'm done with setting myself goals - because then I lose sight of the real reason that I'm doing this, which is to write music that represents me, and have other people feel understood through that music."Image source, Silken WeinbergImage caption, "I pray that one day I'll turn and face the mirror with a smile," sings Humberstone That mindset comes to fruition in the new, expanded edition of Cruel World, whose five new songs were largely written after the original album was handed in."I was super proud of Cruel World and, when you've got that in your back pocket, there's room to experiment and break some of your usual parameters."The new tracks find Humberstone embracing a new persona – more confident, more flirtatious, a little salty – with music inspired by a playlist featuring Abba, Madonna and Robyn.The single Too Cute To Be Lonely, external is a will-they/won't-they story set at a house party."Don't leave a girl upset, in such a pretty dress," she teases the object of her affections.Terminally Yours takes place a couple of weeks later, when Humberstone realises she's fallen head-over-heels in love."Your stupid face is my sorry fate," she harrumphs, cross at herself.  "For [expletive]'s sake, I'm in love."Silver Sky, a gorgeous acoustic ballad, tells another side of the story, as she settles into her lover's arms and drifts into blissful reverie."I wrote that on a kind of Hail Mary trip, seeing what fell out of the air in Nashville," she reveals."We went over to [co-writer Maddie Diaz's] house, took a guitar into the garden and wrote Silver Sky outside, while all of these gorgeous red cardinals were singing around us."I usually write a lot about my mental health struggles, but I was just in the mood to write something that made me feel good."Image source, JME InternationalImage caption, Humberstone won the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, joining the ranks of former winners such as Sam Fender, Florence + The Machine and AdeleNot that her mental health issues are in the rear view mirror. Humberstone admits her stage nerves have only intensified since the release of Cruel World."It's the proudest I've been of any of my work and, for that reason, I struggled with shows because I felt a lot of pressure to go out and deliver it to the standard that I think people are expecting."But on the other hand, it's totally fine if you mess up or sing a wrong note. People can't connect to a pop star that feels too robotic and polished. "So maybe my strength is that vulnerability, and I need to recognise that more."That vulnerability has won Humberstone millions of fans, even if a hit single has (so far) eluded her. And her audience keeps growing.  In May this year, her breakout single Falling Asleep At The Wheel was awarded a silver disc... five years after its release, indicating that her songs have staying power in an era of disposable hits.Astonishingly, this is news to Humberstone, who learns about the accolade during our interview. But it helps to clarify a thought that's been knocking around her head."If I'm going to be doing this for years to come, I've just got to keep making music that feels right, trusting my gut and realising there's no end point," she says."Reaching an end point would mean I've 'made it', but I think, maybe, that's a myth that doesn't really exist."

schema.headline: Holly Humberstone on her identity crisis - and struggle being compared to other pop stars
